It generalizes the SPIHT image coder to the slow growing subdivision refinement structure [S1].

The claim states that the work generalizes the SPIHT image coder to the slow growing subdivision refinement structure. Source [S1] explicitly states in the 'Progressive Compression' section: 'Said and Perlman [13] describe an image coder based on set partitioning in hierarchical trees (SPIHT) that is generalized in this paper to the slow growing subdivision refinement structure.' This directly supports the claim.

The claim states that SGS wavelets are unstable for some settings of alpha. Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.

*   The SPIHT algorithm processes the wavelet coefficients organized in trees [S1].

The claim states that the SPIHT algorithm processes wavelet coefficients organized in trees. The provided evidence explicitly confirms this in multiple places. Section 5.1 states: 'The SPIHT algorithm... exploits the decay behavior of wavelet coefficients as one proceeds from coarse to fine spatial scales by operating on trees of wavelet coefficients.' Additionally, the notes mention that the coder 'operates on trees of coefficients' and discusses 'parent-child relationships' within these trees.

Unlike standard zerotree algorithms that rely on a strict theoretical framework for parent-child relationships, this system applies intuitive spatial relationships analogous to image coding trees to define coefficient hierarchies for subdivision wavelets [S1].

The claim states that unlike standard zerotree algorithms which rely on a strict theoretical framework, this system uses intuitive spatial relationships analogous to image coding trees to define parent-child relationships for subdivision wavelets. Source [S1] explicitly states in Section 5.1: 'There is no theoretical framework that can be used to define such a relationship for subdivision wavelets, but intuitively a definition based on the spatial relationships of parent and child analogous to the trees used in the image coding literature can be applied.' This directly supports every part of the claim.

Thus, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
